title: The wine ran out (John 2:1–11)
hook: at a wedding in Cana Mary tells the servants whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tired fisherman heard but at thy word, and the nets nearly broke with a great draught. Did you try the one thing once more? Day thirty-five, the last day of the week. It ends at a party.

A village wedding in Galilee. Not an afternoon reception: a feast, guests eating and drinking, and the family's honor riding on every cup. Jesus is there, with his first few followers. His mother is there too. And then, somewhere in the middle of it, the thing a host dreads. The wine runs out. The guests don't know yet. The bridegroom may not know yet. But someone has noticed. Not the host, not the steward. Mary. Today: the first sign in John's Gospel, and the woman who saw the need first.
screen: `A VILLAGE WEDDING FEAST.` → `THE WINE RUNS OUT.` → `MARY NOTICES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Mary goes to her son with four words, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." She doesn't tell him what to do. She just names the need. His answer sounds cool to our ears: "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come." Woman wasn't rude in his language. It's the same word he'll use for her from the cross. But he's saying: this isn't my moment. And Mary doesn't argue. She turns to the servants and says: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." Then she steps out of the story. There are six stone water jars standing there, for the Jewish washing rites, holding two or three measures apiece, John says. A great deal of water. Jesus tells the servants: fill them with water. They fill them to the brim. Draw some out, he says, and take it to the chief steward. The steward tastes it, doesn't know where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over, puzzled: everyone serves the good wine first, and the cheap stuff once people have had plenty. "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." Six jars of it. John calls this the beginning of his signs. Catholics treasure it for Mary's sake. Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye: they're the last words John's Gospel gives her, and they point away from herself. Here Catholics see why they ask Mary to pray for them. She notices the need, brings it to her son, and tells everyone else to listen to him. It's the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.
screen: `THEY HAVE NO WINE.` · `MY HOUR IS NOT YET COME.` · `SIX JARS, FILLED TO THE BRIM.` · `THE GOOD WINE, KEPT UNTIL NOW.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back. This week began with a boy lost for three days, then the hidden years, the voice in the desert, the baptism, forty days hungry, and the nets at dawn. Now the wine. Settle and breathe. Think of the rooms you'll be in today: home, work, a group chat. Is there a need nobody has named? Someone running out of something: patience, money, company, hope. Just notice it. If you pray, you can do what Mary did and simply say it: they have no wine. The bell holds the time.
Cana. The village in Galilee where Jesus turned water to wine at a wedding, his mother noticing first.
Your line: do whatever he tells you. Today, when you notice a need, bring it to someone who can help, and then help the way you're asked to. Day thirty-five. Next week: healings and encounters.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the wedding at Cana as the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary and often read it at weddings; Mary's words to the servants are a favorite line for describing her role of pointing to her son.

fork.setup: you're Mary. the wine has run out. you've told your son, and he's said his hour hasn't come. what do you do next?
options: tell the servants to do whatever he tells them.
go and find more wine yourself.
fork.reveal: she turns to the servants: “Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.” and the water jars are filled.

original.note: Greek: woman, a respectful form of address. Jesus calls his mother this at Cana and again from the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus turns water into wine at a party.
what it means: a mother notices a need no one has named, brings it to her son, and tells everyone to listen to him.
what a scholar hears: John calls it the first of the signs; six stone jars, two or three measures apiece, filled to the brim.

sources.quoted: Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come.
Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye.
But thou hast kept the good wine until now.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 2:3, 2:4, 2:5 and 2:10 given from memory; confirm.

Jar capacity: 'two or three measures apiece' (2:6); a measure (metretes) is often estimated at about 9–10 gallons, so 20–30 gallons each and roughly 120–180 in all. The script says 'twenty gallons or more' and 'maybe a hundred and fifty gallons'; confirm.
'Among the last words of hers the Gospels record': Mary appears later (John 19, Acts 1) without recorded speech; confirm phrasing.
Mary's intercession: the script says Catholics 'see here why they ask Mary to pray for them'; confirm it is fairly stated.
Week look-back in the practice lists the week's titles (days 29–35).
The carry and review use the index's modern wording ('do whatever he tells you'); the Douay-Rheims line is quoted in the teach.

Editor review (2026-10-01): gallon conversions ('twenty gallons or more', 'a hundred and fifty gallons') replaced with John's own 'two or three measures apiece' (voice and trapdoor); 'could run for days' and 'the line the Church has never forgotten' cut; 'among the last words of hers the Gospels record' narrowed to John's Gospel, which the text supports.
